lawyer:
M Enayetur Rahim, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner: 
Opposite Party No. 1 ----- Appeared in person and represented himself.
parties:
Madinullah Miah ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Md Abdul Mannan & anr ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
The dispute between the parties relates to a piece of land measuring 0.02¾ acres. It will be referred to, hereinafter, as the case land. It is situated on plot No. 50794, appertaining to MRR Khatian No. 1328, corresponding to PS Khatian No. 1319 in Mouza Char King, previously known as Char Ishwar. This will be referred to, in the' paragraphs that follow as the case holding. One Moqbul Ahmed had owned 0.50 acres of land in the case holding. He died leaving behind a family, comprising his widow, 6 sons and 2 daughters, to succeed him to his estate. Ruhul Amin and Abdul Matin are two of his sons. On 14-9-1989 Ruhul Amin sold 0.02 acres of land from the case holding to Mohammad Abdul Mannan, who thus became a co-sharer by purchase of the case holding. He is the opposite party No. 1 of the instant civil revision. He is an Advocate. He built on the land so purchased a 'baithakkhana', though not as an adjunct to any dwelling quarter. On 4-3-1990 Abdul Matin sold 0.02¾ acres of land from the 'case holding' to Md Madinullah Miah, a stranger to the case holding. This is the case land. This is contiguous to the land held by Mannan and lies next to his 'baithakkhana', This gave Mannan an occasion to file, almost 7 years later an application for pre-emption of the case land and institute the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 1997. It was under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950. He impleaded in it Md Madinullah Miah, the purchaser of the case land as the pre-emptee opposite party No. 1 and Abdul Matin, the vendor of the 'case land' as the vendor opposite party No. 2. Abdul Matin is the opposite party No. 2 in the instant civil revision. He was also a party in the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 59 of 2000.out of which the present civil revision arose. The appeal was against the judgment and order passed in the said Miscellaneous Case No.4 of 1997. Abdul Matin took no part in the proceedings, either in the Courts below or in this Court. 

 2. Madinullah seems to have had a peaceful occupation and quiet enjoyment of the case land, for over six and half years since he had purchased it on 4-3-1990. He might have lost his peace in February 1997 when his next-door neighbour. Mannan, in a bid to acquire the land for himself instituted the said pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 1997 in the Court of the Assistant Judge Hatia, Noakhali. Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 obliges a pre-emptor to file his application for pre-emption, within 4 months either from the date of transfer of the 'case land' to the transferee or from the date of knowledge of such transfer. Mannan found no difficulties, despite a lapse of a period of almost 7 years, in crossing the hurdle of limitation period. He did so; simply asserting that he had come to know of the transfer only on 14-10-1996 and after obtaining a certified copy of the transfer document. He offered no explanation how he had remained so ignorant and for so long since the transfer of a piece of land, adjoining his own land and lying next to his 'baithakkhana', particularly when the vendor of the land was not unknown to him. He did not say what prompted him to obtain the certified copy of the transfer document on 14-10-1996 and not any earlier. He did not disclose the source of his knowledge of the transfer of the land to the pre-emptee. 

 3. Madinullah contested the case by filing a written objection. He pleaded that the case was not maintainable due to defect of parties. He claimed that contrary to the requirements of section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 all the co-sharers of the 'case holding' were not made parties in the case. It is to be noted that the pre-emptor petitioner only impleaded the transferor and the transferee of the 'case land' and no one else as parties in the said Miscellaneous Case. This is despite the fact that he was provided with a list of the co-sharers of the 'case holding' by his adversary. Madinullah also pleaded that the case was barred by limitation, disputing Mannan's claimed late knowledge of the transfer of the case land to the transferee. He averred that the 'case land' was first offered for sale to Mannan. The latter declined the offer and recommended the sale of the property to Madinullah. It was claimed that Mannan had known of the transfer of the case land to Madinullah immediately after the transfer. 

 16. The learned Subordinate Judge, though in his judgment and order referred to the decision of Abdus Samad and others vs Md Sohrab and others, reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 77 = 33 DLR (AD) 113, seems to have had misconceived the ratio decidendi of the case. The Appellate Division, in that case held that, in a pre-emption case the pre-emptor, if after being furnished with the particulars of the co-sharers of the case holding, fails to implead all the co-sharers as parties in the pre-emption case, the case will fail. The decision does not authorise an appellate Court to remand a case to the Court below to cure the defect of parties. Ruhul Islam J, who delivered the judgment, observed, "The provision of law as contained in sub-section (2) [of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950] should be followed without minimising its requirement. The requirement as to making of parties is undoubtedly positive. It is the duty of the pre-emptor to implead the necessary parties; as I have observed above, this requirement of law should be enforced keeping in view the provisions of Order 1, rules 9 and 10; if the pre-emptor after getting an opportunity fails to amend his application by impleading the necessary parties, as pointed out by the pre-emptee, and on evidence if it is found that the application suffers from defect of parties, in that event the application cannot succeed and must be dismissed." I am in no doubt, in view of this decision of our Appellate Division, that the learned Subordinate Judge ought to have dismissed the Miscellaneous Case No.4 of 1997, when he had found defect of parties in it. The defect was brought to the notice of the pre-emptor by the pre-emptee at the earliest opportune moment and yet the pre-emptor took no step to amend his plaint and make all the co-sharers of the 'case holding' parties in the Miscellaneous Case. The learned Subordinate Judge, when he found defect of parties, ought to have dismissed the case, instead of remanding it to the Court below. He ought to have appreciated that Order XLI rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 or any other provisions of law do not permit remand just to enable a party to cure the defect of parties and proceed with a properly constituted suit. I cannot conceive of an order of remand under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. The ends of justice will not be met, but defeated, if indulgence is given to the pre-emptee opposite party and if he is allowed to get away with the pre-emption of his neighbour's land, when he took over six and half years to put in his application for pre-emption, since the transfer of the case land to the transferee. In order to overcome the limitation period he pleaded a very late knowledge of the transfer of the case land to the pre-emptee, but did not put forward a plausible explanation for such late knowledge. Again, though he took nearly seven years to submit his application for pre-emption, he did not care to implead all the co-sharers of the case holding as the parties in it. This is despite the fact that the defect of parties was brought to his attention and he was provided with a list of the co-sharers of the 'case holding."
